metaDescription: Six battery backpack leaf blowers compared on airflow, runtime and battery system, from 600 CFM to 850 CFM, with who each suits.
expertTake: The Ryobi 40V HP 850 CFM backpack is the strongest here and a serious gas replacement for anyone already on that platform, while the EGO LB6003 is the one with the longest claimed runtime from its big included pack. The Greenworks 730 CFM 48V kit is a strong value for large lots. A small yard does not need a battery backpack at all, and a handheld will do.
introParagraphs: A battery backpack puts the cells on your back and the fan in your hands, which solves the one complaint every handheld owner eventually has: fatigue. By moving mass to the hips, it lets a cordless tool work at the same sessions as a gas machine without the fuel, the noise or the starter cord.

The tradeoff is that you are buying batteries as much as a blower. Runtime depends on pack capacity and how hard you run the fan, and quoted figures are usually measured at the lowest setting. Learning to read those claims is the main skill in this category.

products.name: Ryobi 40V HP Brushless Backpack Blower Kit 850 CFM 180 MPH
products.description:
This kit has the highest airflow in the group: 850 CFM at 180 MPH from a 40V HP brushless motor, with a runtime claim of over two hours. Those figures put it in the same working range as a mid-size professional gas backpack, which is why it is the best choice for anyone who wants to retire a gas machine. It ships as a kit, so battery and charger are part of the package.

The runtime claim is a best case, quoted at a lower speed than the top figure, but it still indicates a large energy store. Against the EGO LB6003, it moves 250 CFM more air and 35 MPH faster, and against the 48V Greenworks 730 CFM unit it has more volume at a similar speed.

Use the turbo setting for stubborn patches and the middle of the dial for general work. Keep the harness adjusted so the hip belt carries most of the weight. Clean the intake after each use and store the batteries indoors, partly charged, for the winter.
products.bestFor: Large properties and anyone replacing a gas backpack.
pros: 850 CFM and 180 MPH, the most in this group
Claimed runtime of over two hours
cons: Heavy with batteries on your back
Locks you into the 40V Ryobi family

products.name: Worx WG572 80V Backpack Blower 800 CFM 150 MPH
products.description:
The WG572 takes a different approach to battery power: it draws from four 20V PowerShare packs at once to make an 80V system. That is an unusual advantage, because the same packs fit the brand's trimmers, drills and other 20V tools, so a household can spread the cost across the whole tool shed. The listing quotes a maximum 800 CFM and 150 MPH from a brushless motor.

Its airflow is close to the Ryobi's 850 CFM but its air speed is lower, at 150 MPH against 180 MPH. For dry leaves on grass, that difference is small. For wet leaves, the higher speed of the other models matters.

The price of the flexibility is the pack count: you need four 20V batteries to run it at full strength. Check how many come in the box, since a kit with fewer packs will not reach the top figures. Store packs indoors and keep the intake clear.
products.bestFor: Households with several 20V PowerShare tools already.
cons: Needs four packs for full power

products.name: Greenworks 48V (24V x2) Backpack Blower 730 CFM 185 MPH 2x8.0Ah
products.description:
This Greenworks kit lists 730 CFM and 185 MPH, a high air speed for a battery backpack, with a brushless motor and QuietForce technology aimed at reducing noise. It runs from two 24V packs, and the kit includes two 8.0Ah batteries, which is the largest pairing in the group.

Against the Ryobi 850 CFM kit, it moves 120 CFM less air but is faster than most rivals at 185 MPH, which helps with matted wet leaves. Against the Worx 800 CFM, it has more speed and needs only two packs instead of four.

Turbo and a variable-speed trigger give control. With two 8.0Ah packs, real runtime should be longer than the shorter kits, but the maker does not state a figure, so I will not give one. Clean the intake, charge both packs and store them indoors.
products.bestFor: Large lots with wet leaves where speed matters.
pros: 730 CFM and 185 MPH, a fast stream
cons: Less volume than the 800 and 850 CFM models

products.name: Greenworks 40V Backpack Blower 710 CFM 175 MPH 2x8.0Ah Dual Port
products.description:
The dual-port Greenworks takes two 40V batteries at once, which the maker says extends runtime by 100 percent compared with a single pack. It lists 710 CFM and 175 MPH. The kit includes two 8.0Ah packs and a charger, so the whole system is in the box.

Because the packs run in series, one pack is not used up before the other starts, so there is no hot-swap mid-job. Compared with the 48V Greenworks unit at 730 CFM and 185 MPH, it is a little weaker, but sits on the more common 40V platform that fits other Greenworks tools.

The listing mentions hard surfaces and patios as typical uses, which suits a mid-size lot. Check that both packs seat firmly, since a half-seated pack will cut the tool out, and keep the vents clear. Store packs indoors.
products.bestFor: 40V Greenworks owners wanting twice the runtime from two packs.

products.name: EGO Power+ LB6003 Backpack Blower 600 CFM 145 MPH 7.5Ah
products.description:
The LB6003 is the EGO backpack in the group, listing up to 600 CFM and 145 MPH in turbo mode, with a 56V 7.5Ah battery and charger in the kit. EGO claims up to 180 minutes of runtime on a single charge, the longest claim in this guide, though it comes at a lower speed setting. A variable-speed control adjusts the output.

Its airflow is the lowest in this list, 250 CFM below the Ryobi, so it is not the choice for the heaviest leaf loads. What it offers is a large single battery, a respected platform and quiet operation. It suits a half-acre lot with a mix of dry and moderately wet leaves.

Because one large battery runs the tool, you do not need to manage multiple packs. Keep the battery cool, charge it after use and store it indoors. Spare 56V packs fit other EGO tools if you add them later.
products.bestFor: Half-acre lots wanting a single large battery and long runtime.
cons: Runtime claim is at low speed

products.name: Greenworks Pro 60V Backpack Blower 550 CFM 150 MPH Tool Only
products.description:
The Pro 60V backpack is the older and most affordable Greenworks backpack in this guide. The listing quotes up to 540 CFM and 140 MPH in its features and 550 CFM and 150 MPH in its title, a small inconsistency that is worth checking on the product page. The maker compares it to a 32cc gas blower, a marketing claim not a standard.

It is sold as a bare tool, so you need a 60V battery and charger. That makes it a good fit for owners who already have a 60V pack from a mower or trimmer. Compared with the 710 CFM kit, it moves about 160 CFM less air, which matters on big, wet leaf piles.

The 60V platform is robust, but the packs are bigger and heavier than the newer ones. Treat it as a mid-size lot backpack and keep the intake clear. Store the battery separately and indoors.
products.bestFor: Existing 60V Greenworks owners wanting a cheap way into a backpack.
pros: Backpack comfort at a lower price
540 to 550 CFM on a brushless motor
Harness spreads weight for long sessions

buyingCriteria.explanation: These backpacks use very different battery systems: four 20V packs on the Worx, two 24V or 40V packs on the Greenworks, a single 7.5Ah 56V pack on the EGO and a 40V HP system on the Ryobi. The total stored energy sets the runtime, not the voltage label. A kit with two 8.0Ah packs holds far more than one with a single 4.0Ah. Count the packs in the box and the platform you already own before comparing airflow.

The Ryobi lists 850 CFM at 180 MPH, the Worx 800 CFM at 150 MPH, the Greenworks 48V 730 CFM at 185 MPH and the EGO 600 CFM at 145 MPH. A large CFM moves bulk, while a high MPH lifts wet and matted leaves. For wet autumn leaves, speed deserves more weight than most buyers give it. Look at both figures on every listing.

The EGO claims up to 180 minutes and the Ryobi claims over two hours, but both are at a low speed. At turbo, expect a small fraction of that. A realistic plan is to use the middle of the speed dial for most of the job. Ask yourself how long a typical leaf day takes, and match the claimed number to it with a generous margin.

The whole point of a backpack is the harness, so check what it offers. A padded hip belt and chest strap move weight off your shoulders. Battery packs on your back add several pounds to the load, and two 8.0Ah packs weigh more than one 4.0Ah. If you are short or slight, try a harness before you buy, or look for adjustable torso length.

A big pack takes a long time to charge on a slow charger, which can leave you waiting between sessions. Some kits include a rapid charger, and a spare pack avoids the wait. If you clear every weekend in autumn, the charger matters as much as the blower. Check the charger rating on the listing.

The Greenworks Pro 60V is sold as a bare tool, while the Ryobi, EGO and Greenworks 40V and 48V listings include batteries. A bare tool is a saving if you own compatible packs, but a poor deal otherwise. A battery is usually the largest single part of a kit, so price the full setup.

specDecoder.meaning: Some blowers combine several small packs to make a larger voltage. The Worx uses four 20V packs for 80V and the Greenworks uses two 24V packs for 48V.
specDecoder.watchFor: Without all the packs the tool will not reach its top figures.

specDecoder.meaning: A design that takes two batteries at once. It doubles stored energy and runtime.
specDecoder.watchFor: Both packs must be charged and seated for the tool to run.

specDecoder.meaning: Battery capacity. An 8.0Ah pack holds twice the energy of a 4.0Ah at the same voltage.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EGO's 7.5Ah single pack and the Greenworks' two 8.0Ah packs differ greatly in total energy.

specDecoder.meaning: A short-burst setting that raises airflow above normal. It drains the battery quickly.
specDecoder.watchFor: Peak CFM figures are usually quoted in turbo.

specDecoder.meaning: A marketing comparison to a gas engine size, such as 32cc. It is not a standard measurement.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greenworks Pro 60V uses this claim, so check CFM and MPH instead.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared CFM and MPH across the six backpacks. The Ryobi 850 CFM at 180 MPH leads on both, and the EGO at 600 CFM and 145 MPH is lowest on both. Neither figure was treated alone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Energy and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the number and capacity of batteries in each kit, and the maker's runtime claims. Two 8.0Ah packs or a 7.5Ah pack store far more energy than a small single pack.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform sensibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how each system fits other tools. The Worx four-pack design uses existing 20V packs, and EGO and Greenworks packs fit their own families. Cross-platform value counted heavily.

howWeEvaluated.title: Carry comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted harness features and the weight of batteries on the back. A backpack that is uncomfortable defeats its own purpose, so comfort was weighed alongside output.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we flagged bare tools and the cost of missing packs. A complete kit with a rapid charger earns the most credit for a new buyer.

cards.label: Single large pack
cards.text: The EGO LB6003 uses one 7.5Ah pack. Simple to manage and charge, but one battery to run out.

cards.label: Dual packs
cards.text: The Greenworks dual port and 48V kits use two 8.0Ah packs, and the Worx uses four. More energy and runtime, but more to charge.

howToChoose.note: Take a single pack for lots under an acre; go dual for long sessions.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: High air speed and enough battery to stay at the top of the dial. Wet leaves need speed to peel, and a bigger pack to sustain it.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Greenworks 48V at 185 MPH and the Ryobi at 180 MPH are the best fits. The EGO at 145 MPH and the Worx at 150 MPH are weaker on wet leaves.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You clear more than an acre or want to retire a gas backpack. The Ryobi kit gives the most capability.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a half acre and own a 60V pack. The Greenworks Pro 60V tool only is enough.

maintenance.why: Leaf scraps clog the intake and heat the motor. A quick brush keeps airflow close to rated.
A backpack carries batteries on webbing, so worn straps should be replaced before they fail.

maintenance.task: Charge both packs before a session
maintenance.why: A dual-pack system runs only as long as the weaker pack. Matched, fully charged packs avoid an early cut-out.
Lithium packs degrade when stored full, empty or cold. A dry, mild room keeps them healthy.
Grit on the terminals causes sudden cut-outs under load. A dry cloth keeps them clean.

faq.q: Can a battery backpack replace a gas blower?
faq.a: For most homes, yes. The Ryobi lists 850 CFM at 180 MPH and the Greenworks 48V lists 730 CFM at 185 MPH, comparable to mid-size gas backpacks. For daily commercial use, gas still wins on runtime.

faq.q: How long does the battery last?
faq.a: Claims range from over two hours on the Ryobi to up to 180 minutes on the EGO, all at lower speeds. At turbo, expect a fraction of that.

faq.q: Do I need to buy batteries separately?
faq.a: For the Greenworks Pro 60V, yes. The Ryobi, EGO, Greenworks 40V and 48V listings include batteries and a charger.

faq.q: Why does the Worx need four batteries?
faq.a: It combines four 20V packs to make an 80V system. The benefit is that the packs fit other 20V tools, but all four are needed for top performance.

faq.q: Is speed or volume more important?
faq.a: It depends on the job. Volume moves piles of dry leaves, and speed lifts wet or stuck ones. The best backpacks offer both.
They are much quieter than gas, and some such as the Greenworks 48V mention noise reduction technology. At full turbo they are still loud, so use ear protection.
